sections.html: Scoloplax empousa Schaefer, Weitzman & Britski, 1989. Size: 20 mm (0.8") SL. Type locality: Rio Ivinheima, 70 kilometers upstream from its confluence with Rio Paraná, Mato Grosso State, Brazil. Etymology: Scoloplax comes from the Greek skolos (thorn) and plax (plate), in reference to the moveable dermal bone on top of the snout (rostral plate) studded with large integumentary teeth. Empousa is Greek for a hobgoblin or specter having various forms, in reference to the especially bizarre appearance of the species. IUCN Red List: Least Concern (last assessed 2020).
South America: Amazon and Paraguay/Paraná River basins.

South America: Amazon and Paraguay/Paraná River basins: Bolivia and Brazil. Type locality: Rio Ivinheima 70 km upstream from its confluence with Rio Paraná and Rio dos Bandeirantes, Mato Grosso, Brazil, approx. 22º35'S, 53º30'W.

Facultative air-breathing in the genus; an air-breather, inhabiting clear water streams with sandy to muddy bottom, up to 2.5 m deep with water flow up to 30 cm/sec. When disturbed it may bury itself in the sand, diving quickly headfirst and making lateral movements with the body. Hides during the day amidst the exposed root tangle and basal portions of submersed aquatic vegetation, and among plant debris on the bottom.
Similar maintenance as to the banjo catfishes but due to their small size would need to be kept with small characins etc.
Forages at twilight and night, moving little and preying mostly on chironomid larvae and tiny oligochaetes.
Larger male specimens have large, fleshy tissue at the ventral opening. Females have no tissue sac.
Unreported in the aquarium. There is no breeding report.

A sample of 874 individuals (7.7-16.4 mm SL) taken at the end of the rainy season contains six sexually dimorphic males (14.0-14.6 mm SL) and several presumably adult females (12.8-16.4 mm SL) with up to 300 immature oocytes in each ovary. Sexual ratio of 28 adults (11.9-14.1 mm SL) taken at random is 0.86 males to 1.14 females.

Species of the neotropical family Scoloplacidae are distinguished from other Siluriformes by a conspicuous shield-shaped rostral plate bearing numerous large, recurved odontodes. Scoloplacidae is a monogeneric family endemic to South America, known from the Amazon, Paraguay and Paraná basins. The world's smallest known catfish are from this genus; the smallest is most likely S. dolicholophia.

Scoloplax empousa is distinguished from all other Scoloplax by the combination of paired bilateral mental barbels, four dorsal-fin rays, five pectoral-fin rays, five pelvic-fin rays and six anal-fin rays.

Description: Dorsal soft rays (total): 4; anal soft rays: 6. Paired bilateral barbels.

Etymology: The specific name empousa: Émpousa, in Greek mythology a one-legged specter assuming various forms, referring to this catfish's "rather bizarre external appearance".

Remarks: Despite the few information available on this species, it is assessed as Least Concern due to its wide range (IUCN 2020).
Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia v. 141, pp 194, Figs. 7, 8, 11.
